**On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape:** Sitaram is the loyal palace guard stationed at the inner-quarters door, duty-bound to stop Udayaditya from leaving. He blocks the Yubaraj, but when confronted, refuses to fight him (since Udayaditya once saved his life twice), and instead begs to be disarmed and bound so he can later claim he was overpowered — Udayaditya is the one breaking free, while Sitaram passively submits and lets him pass.

**On the night of Udayaditya's own escape from prison:** the roles invert. Now it is Sitaram who takes the active, initiating role — he is the one who comes to the locked prison amid the chaos of the fire, bursts in, and physically pulls/carries the passive, bewildered Udayaditya out to freedom, with Udayaditya left asking helplessly what he should do and where he should go, now depending entirely on Sitaram's guidance rather than acting on his own.

Pratapaditya's first plan was to have two Pathan men ambush and kill Basanta Ray at the inn in Simultali as the old king traveled to Jessore. This failed because the Pathan assigned the task was so charmed by Basanta Ray's music and kindness that he couldn't bring himself to kill him—instead confessing the plot to Udayaditya, who arrived in time. In the end, Pratapaditya succeeded by sending commander Muktiyar Khan with a signed death order to Raigarh fort, where Basanta Ray, after being shown the order in his uncle's own hand, calmly submitted, and was beheaded by the soldier Abdul on Muktiyar Khan's command.

In the Jessore inner quarters, disguised as a woman (an old nurse/maidservant), where Rammohan seized and nearly strangled him, bound him with a shawl, and carried him out; and later in the king's chamber at Chandradwip, where Rammohan grabbed him by the neck and threw him bodily out of the room.

Rukmini (disguised as the tantric healer Mangala) secretly prepared a poison, which was fetched through Matangini under the guise of medicine to win back Udayaditya's affection, and Surma secretly consumed it, dying—her death being the true cause of her "departure" rather than the ordered exile to her father's house.

Because Vibha refused to go with Rammohan on his first visit, King Ramchandra Ray (her husband), humiliated and angered by her rejection, went ahead and married another woman. So when Vibha finally did go to Chandradwip, she arrived only to find that her husband was marrying someone else that very day, shattering all her hopes of happiness.

Udayaditya, tormented by Rukmini's accusations that he had ruined her, offered to give her anything she wanted. Rukmini asked for the ring on his finger, and he pulled it off and gave it to her. Sitaram and Bhagavat then used that ring, which bore Udayaditya's name engraved as a seal, to stamp a forged petition made to look like Udayaditya was writing to the Emperor in Delhi accusing Pratapaditya of treason and seeking the kingdom for himself. Bhagavat delivered this sealed, forged petition to Pratapaditya, claiming he had intercepted it from a fleeing servant of Udayaditya's, and this fabricated evidence led Pratapaditya to believe his son was betraying him, resulting in Udayaditya's imprisonment.

Ramchandra Ray's nighttime flight left Pratapaditya humiliated and enraged, and he fixated on punishing those connected to it. He sacked Sitaram and Bhagavat for their part in letting Udayaditya through, making Pratapaditya newly watchful of Udayaditya's doings. When Udayaditya and Surma secretly supported the dismissed men, word of it reached Pratapaditya, and his fury over being defied again—this time through Surma's quiet generosity—led him to order Surma sent away to her father's house as retaliation.

The song expresses Basanta Ray's grief at being the sole survivor of a once-joyful, close-knit family—everyone he loved has vanished, leaving him alone with only emptiness and no one left to answer his call. He first sings it wistfully at sunset in Raigarh, alone on his veranda, as nostalgia for his lost loved ones rises unbidden despite his usual cheerfulness. He sings it again at Jessore, standing with Vibha before Surma's silent, empty room, where the song becomes an open lament for the family's shattered joy following Udayaditya's imprisonment and the household's desolation.

Because Rukmini could not prevent Udayaditya's escape with Basanta Ray that night, she ran mad with fury and warned the palace guards, then later accused Basanta Ray, Sitaram, and the Yubaraj of conspiring together. On her word, Pratapaditya came to believe his old uncle had helped steal away the Yubaraj, and he sent Muktiyar Khan with soldiers to Raigarh—ordering that if Udayaditya could not be recaptured, Basanta Ray be put to death. It was this suspicion, born directly from Rukmini's failed attempt to stop the midnight flight and her subsequent accusations, that led to Basanta Ray being executed by the king's order.

Pratapaditya greeted Ramchandra with cold indifference—no fanfare, no music, a modest escort, and a curt, distracted audience where he prioritized tax business over his son-in-law, making Ramchandra feel inferior and insulted. Later, in his own court, Ramchandra reverses this by mocking Pratapaditya as lowborn (grandson of an "earthworm," a jumped-up leech), claiming Pratapaditya's father had to beg Ramchandra's grandfather for royal anointment, and letting his minister and jester daily hurl insults at Pratapaditya to assert his own superiority and honor.

Rukmini—the older widow from Raigarh who had once seduced the young Udayaditya—secretly fled there and settled near Jessore under the new name Mangala, concealing her past. Still driven by jealousy and ambition to one day rule Jessore through Udayaditya, she won the queen's trust as a tantric healer and was called upon to prepare a "remedy" meant to turn the prince's heart from Surma. Instead, she brewed a slow-acting poison, which Surma ultimately took, leading to her death. Later, Rukmini revealed herself to Udayaditya, guilt-tripping him over her ruined life and manipulating him into giving her his ring, plotting further harm against him.

Udayaditya's youthful despair at being crown prince—feeling tested, neglected, and judged unfit by his father, and tormented by his own shame over Rukmini—grows into a lifelong sense of unworthiness that even Surma's love and faith cannot fully heal. When his grand-uncle Basanta Ray is killed as a direct result of actions tied to Udayaditya, his earlier wish never to have been heir crystallizes into unbearable guilt: he concludes he is a "weak coward" whose existence only brings ruin to those he loves. Returning as a prisoner before Pratapaditya, he explicitly declares himself unworthy of the kingdom and asks to be released from the throne, swearing before Ma-Kali that he will never claim or sit upon Jessore's throne, ceding succession to Samaraditya, before departing to live out his life in renunciation at Kashi.

The letter, which Ramchandra Ray wrote renouncing Vibha and demanding she never be sent back, was carried toward Pratapaditya's court by Nayanchand, who—fearing the Maharaj's reaction—gave it instead to the Mahishi. She showed it to Basanta Ray, and both agreed to keep it hidden from Vibha and Pratapaditya. Rather than reveal its true contents, they had it announced throughout the household that Ramchandra Ray had written requesting Vibha be sent back to her in-laws, filling Vibha with joy and trust in her husband's forgiveness.

Pratapaditya tried to seal Ramchandra Ray's only water-route escape by having guards block the palace canal with heavy Sal-wood logs, since his boat was moored there. But Rammohan, carrying Ramchandra on his back, climbed down a rope made of knotted sheets from the roof straight into the boat, bypassing the blocked inner-quarter doors entirely. When the boat reached the log barrier, it simply pulled up and over the logs. The guards, lacking a readied gun and then wasting time fetching a boat (the messenger stopped to smoke and chase a debt before finally returning), never managed to pursue in time—so by the time anyone could react, the boat had already passed the barrier and reached the river, letting Ramchandra escape despite the blockade.

Basanta Ray's sitar was once his constant, cherished companion, a voice for his inner feelings when words failed him; even amid Udayaditya's earlier troubles, he tried to play it, though grief choked his throat and stopped him. Ultimately he renounced it entirely, vowing never to play it again as he parted from Udayaditya. Later, in Raigarh, his beloved instrument sits silent beside him, its strings broken and untunable—he no longer plays it at all. This abandonment of the sitar mirrors his inner state: just as its strings are broken beyond repair, his heart is broken by helplessness over Udayaditya's fate, and the joy and music that once defined him have gone silent, replaced by quiet grief and dread for what has befallen the one he loves like a son.

Before Surma's death, Udayaditya acted boldly on behalf of wronged subjects—going out at night to involve himself in their affairs, defying his father's wishes, and ready to confront danger and oppression without regard for consequences. After Surma dies, this courage collapses into a paralyzing, almost superstitious dread of Pratapaditya. He no longer rides out to stop looting and arson against subjects, cannot bear to intervene even when he witnesses a subject being beaten and pleading for mercy, and hesitates endlessly over small acts like sending money to people in hardship, ultimately failing to act at all.

Sitaram, who as a prison guard had conspired with Bhagavat to forge the petition that got Udayaditya falsely imprisoned, secretly arranges a fire as a diversion at the prison and guard quarters, then uses the chaos to break into Udayaditya's cell, pull him out, and personally lead him to freedom—physically reversing the imprisonment he had helped cause by engineering the Yubaraj's escape.

First, when the enemy had trapped the king and his party on the palace roof above a canal, Rammohan tied Ramchandra Ray to his back, lowered himself hand over hand down a rope improvised from twisted-together bedsheets, gripping it with his teeth once his hands gave out, and carefully set the king down into the waiting boat below before leaping down himself, then rowed the boat over log barricades to escape the pursuing guards.

The second time, after the king publicly spurned and humiliated the grief-stricken Vibha before his jester, Rammohan furiously threw out the mocking jester, rebuked the king to his face for insulting his "lady mother," declared he was quitting royal service, then simply picked up the fainted, exhausted Vibha in his arms, carried her out of the palace to the waiting palanquins, and took her away to the boat for good.

In Jessore she is dressed up as a princess—her mother personally adorns her with heavy gold ornaments: eight thick gold bangles plus a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring forced onto her delicate face, and an elaborate styled hairdo, despite Vibha's own preference for simple, delicate turquoise bangles and no nose ring at all. In Chandradwip, by contrast, she strips away all that royal finery and disguises herself as an ordinary common woman, plainly dressed, with none of the jewels or elaborate styling—so unassuming that even the boat's own servants fail to recognize her and ask in surprise why she is dressed that way.

In his bedchamber, the window is where Surma used to sit, and Udayaditya returns to it hoping, against reason, to find her there—it stands for loss and a grief-filled longing for someone who will never come back, tying him to memory and sorrow. In the prison cell, the window instead faces the open sky and birds, and watching it convinces him that his chains will one day break and he will be free; it becomes a symbol of hope and eventual liberation, so much so that he calls the window his one truly free space, while the comfortable room beyond it, by contrast, feels like his real prison.

Their relationship began as a transactional flirtation: Sitaram, perpetually penniless but full of swagger, courted the moneylending widow Rukmini with playful banter and sweet names purely to borrow silver, while she indulged him with mock affection, never truly expecting repayment. But once Sitaram helped imprison Udayaditya—whom Rukmini considered "her" prince, hers alone to ruin or save—her affection curdled into possessive rage; when he threatened and nearly struck her over the prince's imprisonment, her hidden fury surfaced, and she vowed silent vengeance. After Udayaditya's escape ruined her last hopes, Sitaram, greedy and careless, visited her cottage at night hoping to loot her money, only to find her drenched, wild-eyed, and consumed with hatred. She lunged for a blade to kill him, and he barely escaped with his life, afterward fleeing the city entirely—while she turned fully vindictive, reporting the conspiracy to the king and demanding brutal punishment for everyone involved.

It starts as a simple diversion: Sitaram sets multiple rooms ablaze and sabotages the firefighting efforts of the guards and commoners (dousing where there's no fire, breaking water pots, creating confusion) to clear the way for sneaking Udayaditya out and getting him onto a boat.

Once Udayaditya is safely away, Sitaram escalates the ruse into outright deception: he has his men torch the now-empty prison cell itself, then plants charred bones, a skull, and Udayaditya's sword inside it. He orchestrates panicked shouts of the Yubaraj screaming and the roof collapsing, personally rushing in to announce there's no response—manufacturing convincing "evidence" that Udayaditya perished in the blaze. This turns the original distraction fire into a staged death, buying time for the escape before the truth (through Rukmini's testimony and later sightings) unravels the cover-up.

He makes light of it—mocking Udayaditya alongside the others rather than feeling any gratitude. In court, when Ramai Bhand and the minister ridicule Pratapaditya and his son, Ramchandra joins in laughing at Udayaditya for being Pratapaditya's son, with no acknowledgment that Udayaditya had risked himself to save his life. He dismisses that rescue as something bound to happen regardless, and further assumes Udayaditya acted only for his sister Vibha's sake rather than out of real concern for him—so instead of gratitude, he lets his courtiers mock his brother-in-law, lacking the will to stop them or refrain from joining in.

Early on, Pratapaditya scorns any fear of the Emperor of Delhi's displeasure, boasting that he alone is the Emperor's judge and dismissing his minister's warnings about imperial anger as irrelevant to his plans. Later, Bhagavat and Sitaram exploit this very specter by forging a petition—sealed with Udayaditya's ring—falsely showing the prince accusing Pratapaditya of treason before the Emperor of Delhi to seize the throne. Bhagavat presents this forged "proof" of Udayaditya's betrayal to Pratapaditya, convincing him of his son's disloyalty and leading to the prince's imprisonment.

While Surma was alive, braiding and arranging Vibha's hair was one of the intimate, affectionate tasks that marked her special bond with Vibha—so much so that when the Mahishi over-adorned Vibha for her husband's visit, Vibha secretly sought out Surma to have her hair redone to her own liking, trusting only Surma's gentle touch to make her truly happy and at ease.

After Surma's death, this small ritual becomes a haunting absence. At the hour when her hair would normally be braided, Vibha sits waiting, half-believing Surma will still appear to do it as always—but no one comes, and her hair remains unbraided, evening turning to night. This neglected, undone hair becomes the visible sign of her grief: later, when Rammohan sees her again, he immediately notices her unkempt hair and sorrowful face as proof that no one is left to care for her tenderly the way Surma once did. The simple act of hair-grooming thus becomes a quiet emotional barometer—its careful performance signifying Surma's loving presence, and its abandonment marking the devastating void left by her death.
